header.title: Ὅροι Ἀσκληπιοῦ πρὸς Ἄμμωνα βασιλέα: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Hermetica
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg1286.tlg016.1st1K-grc1, from Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg1286.tlg016.1st1K-gr: Signs follow the edition: ⟨ ⟩ marks the editor's additions and ⟨...⟩ a gap, [ ] words he deletes, ⎡ ⎤ words he marks as doubtful. 'Full of' follows his emendation με[γι]σταῖς, which turns 'greatest' into 'full'.

Signs follow the edition: ⟨ ⟩ marks the editor's additions and ⟨...⟩ or ⟨....⟩ gaps, [ ] words he deletes, ⎡ ⎤ words he marks as doubtful, ⟨⟨ ⟩⟩ words he moves here from elsewhere; moved words are translated only in their new place ('squadrons' in 13, 'But these are certainly few' in 16). τ῀ιΗ in 13 is read as τῇ. 'Instant' in 15 is his restoration ⟨σ⟩τι⟨γ⟩μήν of τιμήν. The clause on reason and love in 16 is corrupt; the sense may be that what these people love is not reason but desire, which strays and leads astray.

nodes.text: But the discourse, expressed in our ancestral language, keeps the meaning of its words clear; for the very quality of the sound ⟨...⟩, and the ⎡power⎤ of Egyptian names holds in itself the efficacy of what is said. As far as is possible for you, then, O king—and you can do all things—keep the discourse untranslated, so that such mysteries may not reach the Greeks, and the ⎡arrogant⎤, slack and, as it were, prettified diction of the Greeks may not make faint the solemnity and solidity and the effective diction of the names. For the Greeks, O king, have [effective] words empty of proofs; and this is ⟨the⟩ philosophy of the Greeks, a noise of words. But we do not use words, but sounds full of [the] deeds.

Under him is ranked the chorus of daemons, or rather choruses; for they are many and varied, ranked under the ⟨command⟩ of the stars, equal in number for each of them. Arranged, then, ⟨in⟩ ⟨⟨squadrons⟩⟩, they serve each of the stars, being good and bad in their natures, that is, in their activities; for the essence of a daemon is activity. [But some of them are mixed of good and bad.]

These, having been allotted authority over all affairs on earth, ⟨.... and they are the causes⟩ also of the disturbances on earth, and they work manifold confusion, both publicly for cities and nations and privately for each person. For they reshape our souls and draw them over to themselves, sitting in our sinews and marrow and veins and arteries [and in the brain itself], reaching even to the very entrails.

For when each of us has been born and ensouled, he is taken over by the daemons who are on duty at that ⟨instant⟩ of birth, who were assigned ⟨under⟩ each of the stars; for these change from instant to instant, not the same ones staying on, but revolving in turn. These, then, entering through the body into the two ⟨irrational⟩ parts of the soul, whirl it about, each towards his own activity. But the rational part of the soul stands free of the daemons' mastery, fit to receive God.

⟨For whomever⟩, then, a ray shines on the rational part [through the sun] ⟨from God⟩, for him the daemons are made powerless; for no one, whether of daemons or of gods, can do anything against a single ray of God. ⟨⟨But these are certainly few.⟩⟩ All the others are led and carried along, both souls and bodies, by the daemons, loving and cherishing their activities; and love not ⟨having⟩ reason ⟨...⟩ is, the one that strays and leads astray. This whole earthly ⎡government⎤, then, they govern through the instruments of our bodies. And this government Hermes called Fate.
